summary: Design a set with O(1) average insert, remove and getRandom.
mainInsight: Keep values in a list for O(1) random indexing plus a dict from value to its list index. To remove, swap the element with the last one, update the moved element's index, pop the last, and delete the key.

approaches.name: List only
approaches.summary: Insert by append; remove by list.remove.

approaches.name: Dict only
approaches.summary: Hash set; random choice via list(set).

personalSolution.approach: List + dict of indices with swap-with-last removal
personalSolution.notes: Optimal and the update order is safe, including when the removed value is the last element.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to update the moved element's index
Returning the wrong boolean for duplicates

cards.answer: A list of values plus a hash map from value to list index, removing by swapping with the last element. Clue: Every operation must take constant time on average: a hash map gives lookups but random picking needs an array index, so combine them and remove by swapping with the last element.
keyPoints: Every operation must take constant time on average: a hash map gives lookups but random picking needs an array index, so combine them and remove by swapping with the last element.
cards.explanation: The array gives uniform random access, the map finds an element's position, and swapping with the last element removes without shifting.

promptVariants: Which two structures give O(1) insert, remove and getRandom?
Why is one data structure not enough?
options: A list for indexing and a dict from value to index
A heap for removal and a stack for random choice
A sorted array and a binary search tree
Two hash sets that mirror each other
cards.answer: A list for indexing and a dict from value to index
cards.explanation: The list gives random index access; the dict finds an element's index.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Two hash sets that mirror each other: Hash sets cannot pick a random element in O(1).

promptVariants: Why swap with the last element before popping?
cards.answer: Deleting from the middle of a list is O(n) because of shifting. Instead the element to remove is overwritten by the last element, the dict entry of the moved element is updated to the new index, and the last slot is popped (O(1)). Order does not matter in a set, so this is allowed.
cards.explanation: Handle the case where the removed element is the last one.

promptVariants: Trace your remove(val) when val is the last element of arr. Why does it still leave the structure consistent?
What would go wrong if `del self.hmap[val]` ran before `self.hmap[last] = idx`?
cards.code:
def remove(self, val: int) -> bool:
    if val not in self.hmap:
        return False
    idx = self.hmap[val]
    last = self.arr[-1]
    self.arr[idx] = last
    self.hmap[last] = idx
    self.arr.pop()
    del self.hmap[val]
    return True
cards.answer: When val is the last element, idx is the last index and last == val: arr[idx] = last rewrites the same value, hmap[last] = idx rewrites the same entry, pop removes it, and the final del removes the key. If the del ran first, hmap[last] = idx would re-create the key for the removed value, leaving a stale entry that makes insert(val) return False although val is gone.
keyPoints: Deleting first lets hmap[last] = idx resurrect it
cards.explanation: The order 'move, update index, pop, delete key' is safe for every case.

promptVariants: What goes wrong if you remove the last element without checking whether it is the one being removed?
When the value being removed is already the last element, what can go wrong and which order of updates avoids it?
options: A stale dict key can remain; move last into place, update, then delete
Nothing; the swap works the same when both indices are equal here
The list would become unsorted and getRandom would fail for good
The dictionary would raise a KeyError on the very next insert call
cards.answer: A stale dict key can remain; move last into place, update, then delete
cards.explanation: Delete the key after the index update so a single-element removal still ends consistent.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Nothing; the swap works the same when bo: The stale-key ordering matters when they are equal.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The list would become unsorted and getRa: The list does not need to be sorted.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The dictionary would raise a KeyError on: The first insert has nothing to do with it.

promptVariants: Why not keep only a hash set and call random.choice(list(s))?
What does each single-structure design cost?
cards.answer: A hash set alone gives O(1) insert and remove but random.choice(list(s)) copies the set, so getRandom is O(n). A list alone gives O(1) insert and getRandom but remove must search and shift, O(n). Combining a list (random index) with a dict (value to index) gives O(1) average for all three.
cards.explanation: Each structure covers the operation the other is bad at.
